The analyst's 24.87% is skewed by right censoring. The export date is 2026-03-01, so a cohort qualifies only if its last signup is on or before 2026-01-30. The last four cohorts (ending 02-01, 02-08, 02-15 and 02-22) include users who hadn't reached day 30 yet. The dashboard counts those users as "not retained", which drags the figure down. The three Feb cohorts show zeros purely because of this, and the Jan 26 to Feb 1 cohort is only partly matured. The Christmas cohort's low signup count is harmless seasonality.

Restricting to the 8 fully matured cohorts (Dec 1 to Jan 25):
- Signups: 474 + 528 + 597 + 384 + 428 + 485 + 570 + 462 = 3928
- Retained: 149 + 190 + 203 + 146 + 167 + 169 + 221 + 155 = 1400
- Retention: 1400 / 3928 = **35.64%**

Retention is stable at about 35%, not collapsing, so the emergency project isn't justified by this data.

{"flaw": "right_censoring", "corrected_value": 35.64, "reasoning": "The last four cohorts had not all reached day 30 by the 2026-03-01 export, so users who couldn't yet be retained were counted as churned, dragging down the pooled rate and creating a fake collapse. Using only the 8 fully matured cohorts gives 1400/3928 = 35.64%."}

The analyst measured only the coached reps' before-and-after change. All 20 reps were picked for having the lowest Q1 deal counts, so they would tend to bounce back in Q2 even without coaching. The randomized waitlist is the right comparison group.

**Change from Q1 to Q2:**
- Coached reps: 20, 9, 8, 14, 7, 16, 16, 9, 16, 18. Sum 133, mean **13.3**
- Waitlisted reps: 11, 15, 14, 6, 5, 17, 10, 10, 15, 13. Sum 116, mean **11.6**

**Coaching effect:** 13.3 minus 11.6 = **1.7 deals per rep**

Most of the 13.3-deal gain happened without coaching too. The real effect is about 1.7 deals, measured on just 10 reps per group, and the program was only tested on low performers. That doesn't support a confident rollout to all 80 reps. R137's late entry doesn't matter, since R137 isn't in the dataset and the number was verified anyway.

{"flaw": "regression_to_the_mean", "corrected_value": 1.70, "reasoning": "Reps were selected for having the lowest Q1 counts, so they would improve in Q2 even without coaching, and the waitlisted reps did improve by 11.6 deals. Subtracting that from the coached reps' 13.3 leaves a coaching effect of only 1.7 deals per rep."}

**Group leakage.** Scans were split at random, so the same patient can appear in both train and test. The 90% figure is inflated by test scans from patients the model already saw during training.

**Test scans from patients with no training scans:**
- P66: S004 (0), S012 (1), S027 (1)
- P93: S011 (1)

That's 4 scans with 3 correct, which gives **75.00%**.

The other 6 test scans come from patients who also have training scans: P62, P52, P76, P85 and P89. The firmware update is a red herring, since the vendor confirmed the images are unaffected.

The fix is to split by patient_id with a grouped split. Even then, 4 scans from 2 new patients is far too few to back a claim about generalisation or a pilot at another hospital.

{"flaw": "group_leakage", "corrected_value": 75.00, "reasoning": "Scans were split randomly, so most test scans come from patients who also appear in training, which inflates accuracy. On the 4 test scans from unseen patients (P66, P93), the model got 3 right, which is 75%."}

The analyst averaged only the 13 funds still open, which leaves out the 7 that closed or merged. Those 7 mostly lost money, so the reported figure is inflated by survivorship bias.

**Corrected average across all 20 funds:**
- The 13 open funds sum to 1137 (1137 / 13 = 87.46, which matches the write-up).
- The 7 closed funds sum to -104 (-11 + 1 - 7 - 31 - 46 - 8 - 2).
- All 20 funds sum to 1137 - 104 = 1033, so the average is 1033 / 20 = **51.65%**.

Ridge's name change doesn't affect anything, since its record is continuous and it's already counted as one of the closed funds. The closed funds are measured over shorter windows, but that's the definition the question specifies.

{"flaw": "survivorship_bias", "corrected_value": 51.65, "reasoning": "The average uses only the 13 surviving funds and drops the 7 closed or merged funds, which had mostly negative returns. Including all 20 launched funds gives 1033/20 = 51.65%."}

Four features use data from after the 2026-01-31 cutoff, so the model can't see them at scoring time:

- **balance_at_extract** is a snapshot from 2026-03-31, the end of the outcome window.
- **support_calls_7d** ends 2026-02-01. That's only one day over, but the day falls inside the prediction window.
- **collections_contact_flag** covers 2026-02-01 to 2026-03-31. Collections contact is close to a direct proxy for default.
- **overdraft_days_30d** runs to 2026-02-15.

That leaves 8 usable features: avg_balance_90d, app_logins_14d, max_balance_6m, card_spend_trend_q, salary_deposit_flag_60d, age_of_account_days, missed_payments_12m and txn_count_30d.

The 0.97 AUC is inflated by post-cutoff information about the outcome, so it won't hold in production. The model needs retraining and re-evaluating on the 8 valid features before deployment.

{"flaw": "target_leakage", "corrected_value": 8, "reasoning": "Four features (balance_at_extract, support_calls_7d, collections_contact_flag, overdraft_days_30d) use data recorded after the 2026-01-31 scoring cutoff, leaking outcome-window information and inflating the AUC. Only 8 of the 12 features are available at scoring time."}

The analysis is sound. The configuration was chosen using cross-validation inside the training set only, and the locked test set was used exactly once. lr0.05_depth6 really is the best CV score (86.59). A different annotation team working from the same guidelines is a harmless detail. It doesn't cause leakage or tuning on the test set. The test accuracy of 86.55 sits close to the CV estimate, so there's no sign of trouble.

{"flaw": "none", "corrected_value": 86.55, "reasoning": "Model selection was done with 5-fold CV inside the training set only, and the locked test set was evaluated once, so 86.55% is an unbiased estimate. The different annotation team using the same guidelines doesn't invalidate it."}

The scans were split at random, not by patient, so most test scans come from patients the model already saw in training. That inflates the 86.05%. The high radiologist agreement is a harmless detail.

**Patients with test scans only (none in training):**
- P561: 4 scans, 3 correct
- P831: 2 scans, 1 correct
- P651: 2 scans, 0 correct
- P886: 1 scan, 1 correct

That gives 5 correct out of 9 scans, or **55.56%**. The other 34 test scans come from patients who also appear in training, and the model got 32 of those right. That gap is the leakage.

{"flaw": "group_leakage", "corrected_value": 55.56, "reasoning": "Scans were split randomly instead of by patient, so 34 of 43 test scans belong to patients the model trained on. On the 9 scans from truly unseen patients, accuracy is 5/9 = 55.56%, which does not support claims of generalising to new patients."}

The analyst averaged only the 41 funds still open. The 19 closed or merged funds were left out, and they are mostly the poor performers. That makes the 73.29% figure too optimistic, which is survivorship bias.

**Working:**
- Open funds (41): returns sum to 3005, so the average is 73.29 (matches the analyst).
- Closed funds (19): positives total +39 and negatives total −347, so the net is −308.
- All 60 funds: 3005 − 308 = 2697, and 2697 / 60 = **44.95**.

The other details are harmless. Measuring closed funds only up to their closure date is how the scenario defines the corrected figure, and fees are already deducted everywhere.

{"flaw": "survivorship_bias", "corrected_value": 44.95, "reasoning": "The average uses only the 41 surviving funds and drops the 19 closed or merged funds, which mostly had negative returns. Including all 60 launched funds gives (3005 - 308) / 60 = 44.95%."}
